slides.title: Building blocks
slides.oldHtml:
Mini-whiteboard: Building blocks

1. Carbohydrates are made of…
Simple sugars (C, H, O)
2. Proteins are made of…
Amino acids (C, H, O, N)
3. Lipids are made of…
1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids
4. Which element is ONLY in proteins?
Nitrogen (N)

slides.title: Too hot!
slides.oldHtml:
Quick check: Too hot!

Whiteboards: At 70 °C, why does the enzyme stop working?
AThe enzyme gets killed / dies
BIts active site changes shape (denatured)
CAll of the enzyme has been used up
⚠ EXAMINER TRAP: Enzymes are NOT alive — NEVER say “killed” or “dies”!

lessons.subject: chemistry
lessons.title: Covalent bonding

slides.title: Two kinds of covalent structure
slides.oldHtml:
Two kinds of covalent structure

Sharing electrons can build either tiny separate molecules or one giant network
Simple molecular
  • Small, separate molecules (e.g. H₂O, CO₂, CH₄)
  • Weak forces between molecules → low m.p. & b.p.
Giant covalent
  • Millions of atoms bonded together (e.g. diamond, graphite, SiO₂)
  • Strong covalent bonds throughout → very high m.p. & b.p.

slides.title: Boiling water
slides.oldHtml:
Quick check: Boiling water

Whiteboards: When water boils at 100 °C, what is broken?
ACovalent bonds between H and O atoms
BWeak intermolecular forces between H₂O molecules
CIonic bonds between H⁺ and O²⁻ ions
⚠ EXAMINER TRAP: NEVER say covalent bonds break on boiling!

slides.title: Giant covalent structures
slides.oldHtml:
Giant covalent structures

Millions of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds
  • Giant lattice — no charged ions
  • Very high m.p. & b.p. — many strong bonds to break
  • Insoluble — no conduction (except graphite)
Why Carbon?
Group 4 → 4 outer electrons → forms 4 strong covalent bonds in every direction! (Silicon too: quartz SiO₂)
1 carbon → 4 strong covalent bonds → endless 3D network
Quartz (SiO₂) — giant covalent too
slides.newHtml:
Giant covalent structures

Millions of non-metal atoms joined by strong covalent bonds
  • Giant lattice — no charged ions
  • Very high melting and boiling points — lots of energy needed to break strong bonds
  • Insoluble in water — does not conduct (except graphite)
Why is Carbon so good at this?
Carbon (Group 4) has 4 outer electrons, forming 4 strong covalent bonds in every direction (silicon does too: quartz SiO₂).
1 carbon → 4 strong covalent bonds → endless 3D network
Quartz (SiO₂) — giant covalent too

slides.title: Fullerenes (e.g. C60)
slides.oldHtml:
Fullerenes (e.g. C60)

Hollow simple covalent molecules of carbon
  • C60 (buckminsterfullerene): hollow ball of 60 carbon atoms — a buckyball
  • Separate molecules held by weak intermolecular forces → soft, slide/roll easily, lower m.p. than diamond
  • Does not conduct electricity — electrons cannot jump between separate C60 molecules
  • Huge surface area & hollow interior (plus nanotubes!)
  • Uses: lubricants, catalysts, targeted drug delivery
C60 buckyball (60 C atoms)
Carbon nanotube

slides.title: Which carbon?
slides.oldHtml:
Mini-whiteboard: Which carbon?

Diamond
Graphite
C60
1. Extremely hard — 4 strong bonds per carbon
→ Diamond
2. Conducts electricity — delocalised electrons
→ Graphite
3. Hollow ball of 60 atoms — simple molecule
→ C60 fullerene
4. Soft & slippery — weak forces between layers
→ Graphite
